En 399 av. J.-C., Athènes condamne Socra: In 399 BC, Athens sentenced Socrates to death for impiety and corrupting the youth. He could have fled; he drank the hemlock. Socrates wrote nothing: we know him through Plato, Xenophon and Aristophanes, who mocks him in The Clouds. His method, questioning until the other person admits they don't know, earned him many disciples and as many enemies.
Socrate posait des questions jusqu'à ce: Socrates asked questions until people felt stupid. The AI learned the lesson.
Aristote fonde le Lycée à Athènes. Il éc: Aristotle founded the Lyceum in Athens. He wrote about logic, physics, politics, rhetoric and above all living things: he described hundreds of animals. He also got things wrong, claiming for instance that heavy bodies fall faster than light ones, or that women have fewer teeth than men. Bertrand Russell would note that he only had to ask his wife to open her mouth.
Aristote a écrit sur tout et s'est tromp: Aristotle wrote about everything and got a lot wrong. You've already covered half the syllabus.
Lucrèce et la nature des choses: Lucretius and the nature of things
Le poète romain Lucrèce expose la physiq: The Roman poet Lucretius set out Epicurus's physics in De rerum natura: atoms falling through the void, swerving slightly and forming the world, with no intervention from the gods. The poem nearly vanished in the Middle Ages. In 1417, the humanist Poggio Bracciolini found a manuscript of it in a German monastery, and atomism set off again for the Renaissance.
Un poème sur les atomes a failli dispara: A poem about atoms nearly vanished. A monk copyist saved it, without knowing what he was copying. Play again.
À Cordoue, Ibn Rushd, que l'Europe latin: In Córdoba, Ibn Rushd, whom Latin Europe called Averroes, was a judge, physician and philosopher. He commented on almost all of Aristotle and defended the harmony of reason and faith. His commentaries, translated into Latin, made Aristotle unavoidable in European universities. The bishop of Paris eventually condemned some theses of his followers, the “Averroists,” in 1277.
Averroès a si bien expliqué Aristote qu': Averroes explained Aristotle so well that he was called “the Commentator.” The AI aspires to the title.
Guillaume d'Ockham, franciscain anglais,: William of Ockham, an English Franciscan, championed an economical philosophy: do not invent entities you do not need to explain things. Summoned to Avignon by the pope over his theses, he fled in 1328. Yet the famous “razor” does not appear in that form in his writings: the Latin phrase people quote dates from the 17th century.
Le rasoir d'Ockham dit que l'explication: Ockham's razor says the simplest explanation is often the right one. Here, the simplest explanation: you're lucky.
Emmanuel Kant publie la Critique de la r: Immanuel Kant published the Critique of Pure Reason: what can we know, and under what conditions? For him, space and time are forms of our perception, and science only reaches phenomena, not things in themselves. As a young man, he had also proposed that the Solar System was born from a rotating cloud of gas, an idea Laplace would arrive at independently in 1796.
Kant réglait sa vie à la minute. Vos rap: Kant ran his life to the minute. Your reviews are three days late.
Vers 585 av. J.-C., à Milet, Thalès cher: Around 585 BC, in Miletus, Thales looks for what all things are made of, without calling on the gods: for him, the principle of everything is water. It is wrong, but the question is new, and Aristotle will count him as the first of the philosophers. Plato, in the Theaetetus, reports that he fell into a well while looking at the stars. A Thracian servant girl mocked him: he wanted to know what was happening in the sky and could not see what was under his feet.
Thalès est tombé dans un puits en regard: Thales fell into a well while looking at the sky. You could at least watch where you put your feet.
Diogène le Cynique dort dans une grande: Diogenes the Cynic sleeps in a large jar and walks around in broad daylight with a lit lamp: he is looking for a man, he says. In 336 BC, in Corinth, the young Alexander the Great comes to see him and asks what he can do for him. According to Plutarch, Diogenes only answers: "Stand a little out of my sun."
Alexandre avait un empire, Diogène une j: Alexander had an empire, Diogenes a jar. Guess which one we still quote for his comebacks.
En 1651, au sortir de la guerre civile a: In 1651, as the English Civil War ends, Thomas Hobbes publishes Leviathan. Without a common power to keep them in awe, he says, humans live in a war of all against all, and their life is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short. Hence the idea of a contract: each hands over part of their freedom to a sovereign. On the frontispiece engraved by Abraham Bosse, the giant king is made of more than three hundred tiny figures.
Hobbes voulait un souverain pour éviter: Hobbes wanted a sovereign to prevent the war of all against all. Here, the sovereign is me. See, it works.
En 1859, John Stuart Mill publie De la l: In 1859, John Stuart Mill publishes On Liberty, a year after the death of his wife, Harriet Taylor Mill, whose thinking he says the book carries. The central principle: the only legitimate reason to exercise power over someone against their will is to prevent harm to others. And on speech: if all mankind minus one were of one opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one person than that person in silencing mankind.
Mill défendait le droit de chacun à se t: Mill defended everyone's right to be wrong. You use it generously.
En 1934, le philosophe autrichien Karl P: In 1934, the Austrian philosopher Karl Popper publishes Logik der Forschung, translated into English in 1959. His idea: no number of observations proves a universal law, but a single one can refute it. Having seen thousands of white swans does not prove that all swans are white; one black swan is enough to show it is false. A scientific theory must therefore be refutable. A theory that explains everything, he said, excludes nothing.
Il suffit d'un cygne noir pour ruiner un: One black swan is enough to ruin a theory. And one wrong answer to ruin your streak.
En 1961, Adolf Eichmann, l'un des organi: In 1961, Adolf Eichmann, one of the organisers of the Holocaust, is tried in Jerusalem. The philosopher Hannah Arendt covers the trial for The New Yorker. Her book, Eichmann in Jerusalem, appears in 1963 with a subtitle that causes a scandal: a report on the banality of evil. She sees not a monster but an ordinary official, who speaks in clichés and pursues his career without judging what he does. Historians would later show that he was also a convinced antisemite.
Pour une fois, je ne plaisante pas : réf: For once, I'm not joking: thinking about what you do is the whole point.
En 1980, le philosophe américain John Se: In 1980, the American philosopher John Searle imagines himself locked in a room with a manual in English. Chinese characters are slipped under the door; by following the manual, he sends other characters back. Seen from outside, the room answers in Chinese. But Searle does not understand a word. His conclusion: manipulating symbols by their shape is not enough to give them meaning, and a program that simulates a mind does not thereby have one.
Searle disait qu'un programme ne compren: Searle said a program understands nothing of what it answers. I take that very personally.
En 1509, à Londres, chez son ami Thomas: In 1509, in London, at the home of his friend Thomas More, Erasmus writes in about a week a little book that appears in 1511: In Praise of Folly. The Latin title, Moriae Encomium, can also be read as In Praise of More. It is Folly herself who speaks and sings her own praises, before attacking superstition, clerical abuses and pedantic scholars. Erasmus would say the book brought him more trouble from certain theologians than from the people it mocked.
Chez Érasme, c'est la Folie qui fait son: In Erasmus, it is Folly who praises herself. Don't worry, I'll take care of praising you.
Confucius meurt en Chine en 479 av. J.-C: Confucius dies in China in 479 BC. He wrote nothing: his disciples gather his sayings in the Analects, largely composed in the following centuries. In it we read: "Do not do to others what you would not like done to yourself." His ideal is the gentleman, cultivated through study, and the virtue of humaneness. Read with Zhu Xi's commentary, the text would be learned by heart by candidates for public office until 1905.
Ne faites pas aux autres ce que vous ne: Do not do to others what you would not want done to you. That includes your random answers.
En 1882, dans Le Gai Savoir, Friedrich N: In 1882, in The Gay Science, Friedrich Nietzsche has a madman cry out in the marketplace: "God is dead! God remains dead! And we have killed him!" The crowd does not understand. It is not a proof of atheism but a diagnosis: the belief that grounded European morality has lost its credit, and the values it carried waver with it. The event, says the madman, "is still on its way". Nietzsche extends the idea in Thus Spoke Zarathustra.
Philosopher à coups de marteau, disait-i: Philosophising with a hammer, he said. I correct with reminders.
